summary: Deprecates the use of the Router Alert Option (RAO) in MPLS echo request and reply messages (LSP ping) from RFC 8029. In practice the RAO was neither required nor used, and RFC 6398 describes security problems with it. It updates RFC 8029.

eli5.summary: A special flag on mail told every office to stop and inspect it, but nobody used it and it caused trouble. This says to stop attaching the flag.

questions: what is the router alert option
subtitle: LSP ping no longer needs the IP Router Alert Option, and gets a proper IPv6 loopback address.

tldr.problem: RFC 8029 required LSP ping messages to carry a Router Alert Option, but it was neither required nor used in practice, and RFC 6398 identifies security vulnerabilities with it outside controlled environments.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9570 removes the option from MPLS echo requests, removes Reply Mode 3, tells implementations to ignore the option on arrival, and recommends the IPv6 loopback address ::1/128 as the destination.
tldr.outcome: The IPv6 RAO value 69 for MPLS OAM and Reply Mode 3 are marked deprecated, and RFC 7506 is explained as reclassified Historic. It updates RFC 8029.

today: RFC 9570 is a Proposed Standard from May 2024 that updates RFC 8029. It is not obsoleted or updated by a later RFC according to the metadata, and it explains why RFC 7506 was reclassified as Historic.

sections.title: LSP Ping and the Router Alert Option
sections.content:
LSP ping (RFC 8029) detects data-plane failures in MPLS Label Switched Paths. In ping mode it checks connectivity; in traceroute mode it traces the path and localizes failures to a node along it.

It uses an MPLS echo request probe and an MPLS echo reply response, both encapsulated in UDP and IP. In ping mode a single request is sent with the MPLS TTL set to 255. In traceroute mode the MPLS TTL is manipulated so that each message expires on a successive router.

RFC 8029 said the IP header of the request must include a Router Alert Option (RAO), and the reply too in one reply mode. This document explains why the RAO was not needed, notes that RFC 6398 recommends against it outside controlled environments, and updates RFC 8029 to retire it.
sections.eli5: LSP ping is like sending a test message down a road to see if every stop is working. It used to carry a special sticker that was not really needed.

sections.title: Why the Echo Request Does Not Need the RAO
sections.content:
An echo request must pass every node in the LSP under test but must not go beyond the egress router. RFC 8029 defined three mechanisms used together to prevent leaking. First, the IPv4 destination is from 127/8 (or a mapped range for IPv6). Second, the IPv4 TTL or IPv6 Hop Limit is 1. Third, the header includes an RAO.

All three were required, but any one is enough to stop the packet being forwarded beyond the egress router. So the document removes requirement 3. No implementation relying on the RAO for this purpose has been reported to the MPLS Working Group.
sections.eli5: Three different locks kept the test message from leaving the building. One lock is enough, so the extra one can go.

sections.title: Removing Reply Mode 3
sections.content:
RFC 8029 defines four reply modes: do not reply, reply via an IPv4/IPv6 UDP packet, reply via a UDP packet with Router Alert, and reply via an application-level control channel.

Mode 3 was suggested for cases where the normal IP return path is deemed unreliable. The RFC calls its rationale questionable, if not wholly misguided, because it is not clear the RAO makes the return path more reliable and it can reduce reliability through the extra processing burden. Mode 3 is removed, and no implementations of it have been reported.
sections.eli5: One way of replying added a special sticker supposedly to help the reply arrive, but it probably slowed it down. That way is dropped.

sections.title: Changes to RFC 8029
sections.content:
RFC 8029 had required the IPv6 destination address of an echo request to come from the IPv4 loopback range mapped into IPv6, which does not behave like an IPv4 loopback packet under RFC 1122. Since RFC 4291 defines ::1/128 as the single IPv6 loopback address, the new text says ::1/128 SHOULD be used. A sender MAY still choose from the mapped range 0:0:0:0:0:FFFF:7F00/104.

To exercise all paths in an ECMP environment, a source of entropy other than the destination address SHOULD be used, for example the MPLS Entropy Label (RFC 6790) or the IPv6 Flow Label (RFC 6438).

Section 2.2 of RFC 8029 is replaced with the rule that implementations SHOULD ignore RAO options on incoming echo requests and replies. The text requiring RAO in Reply Mode 3 is removed, and the requirement in Section 4.3 changes from MUST be set to MUST NOT be set.
sections.eli5: The test message now uses the standard 'this computer only' address, and receivers just ignore the old sticker if they see it.

sections.title: RFC 7506 Reclassified as Historic
sections.content: RFC 7506 defined the IPv6 Router Alert Option for MPLS OAM. This document explains why that RFC has been reclassified as Historic. The section itself is brief and points to the reasons for retiring the RAO from LSP ping given in the other sections.
sections.eli5: The special sticker had its own rule book. Since the sticker is no longer used, that rule book goes on the shelf as history.

sections.title: Backwards Compatibility
sections.content:
Conforming LSP ping implementations SHOULD ignore RAO options on incoming echo requests and replies. This will not harm backwards compatibility because other mechanisms are also used by all legacy implementations in the messages they send and receive.

The IPv6 RAO value for MPLS OAM (69) and Reply Mode 3 are deprecated. In this context, per RFC 8126, deprecated means the values SHOULD NOT be used in new implementations, and deployed implementations that already use them continue to work seamlessly.
sections.eli5: Older devices keep working because they already have other safety measures. New devices just stop using the old sticker.

sections.title: IANA Actions and Security
sections.content:
IANA has marked the IPv6 RAO value for MPLS OAM (69) as DEPRECATED, and has marked Reply Mode 3 in the MPLS LSP Ping Parameters registry as DEPRECATED.

On security, the document states that its recommendations do not compromise security, and that using the IPv6 loopback address ::1/128 strengthens security for LSP ping because it is standardized and has well-defined behavior.
sections.eli5: The official lists now mark the old sticker and the old reply way as 'do not use'. Using the standard home address is also a bit safer.

items.title: Loopback destination
items.text: IPv4 destination from 127/8, so hosts and routers do not forward it.

items.title: TTL of 1
items.text: IPv4 TTL or IPv6 Hop Limit equal to 1.
